Upon the hearth lay two or three thick, lengthy locks of grey human hair, likewise stained with blood, and apparently torn out at the roots. On the floor were discovered four Napoleons, a topaz ear-ring, three large spoons of silver, three smaller ones of métal d’Alger, and two bags holding almost four thousand francs in gold. The drawers of a bureau standing in a corner were open and appeared to have been searched, though numerous articles remained within. Beneath the bed (not beneath the bedstead) a little iron safe was found. This stood open, its key still in the door. Nothing was inside except some old letters and a few other unimportant papers.

“Of Madame L’Espanaye there was no sign here; but an uncommon amount of soot in the fire-place prompted a search of the chimney, from which (dreadful to tell!) the daughter’s corpse was drawn, head foremost downward; it had been driven in that position a considerable way up the narrow opening. The body remained quite warm. Examination revealed numerous abrasions, doubtless caused by the force used in thrusting it upward and pulling it free. Many deep scratches marked the face; on the throat were dark bruises and pronounced impressions of finger nails, suggesting that the deceased had been strangled.

“After carefully examining every part of the house without further discovery, the party proceeded into a small paved yard behind the building. There the old lady’s corpse was lying, her throat cut so completely through that, when they attempted to lift her, the head dropped off. Both head and body were horribly mutilated—the latter to such an extent that it scarcely preserved a human appearance.

“To this dreadful mystery there is, we believe, as yet not the smallest clew.”

The following day’s paper supplied these further particulars.

“‘The Tragedy in the Rue Morgue.’—Numerous persons have been questioned concerning this most extraordinary and appalling affair” [In France the word ‘affaire’ does not yet possess the frivolous significance it bears among ourselves], “but absolutely nothing has emerged to illuminate it. Below we present all the important testimony obtained.

“Pauline Dubourg, laundress, states that she has known the two deceased for three years, throughout which time she did their washing. The old lady and her daughter appeared to live on good terms—showed great affection for one another. Paid remarkably well. Could say nothing as to their manner or means of livelihood. Thought Madame L. earned her living by telling fortunes. Was said to have laid money aside.

A little past noon the boys borrowed a small skiff belonging to a citizen who was away, and set off immediately. Several miles below “Cave Hollow,” Tom spoke:

“Now, you notice this bluff looks just the same all the way down from the cave hollow—no houses, no wood-yards, and the bushes all alike. But see that white patch up there where the ground’s slid down? Well, that’s one of my signs. We’ll go ashore here.”

They landed.

“Now, Huck, from where we’re standing you could reach the hole I came out of with a fishing-pole. See whether you can find it.”

Huck hunted all around the spot without finding anything. Tom strode proudly into a dense clump of sumach and said:

“There it is! Just look, Huck; there ain’t a snugger hole in the country. Mind you keep quiet about it. I’ve wanted to be a robber all this time, but I knew I’d need something like this, and finding it was the trouble. Now we’ve got it, and we’ll keep it secret, except we’ll tell Joe Harper and Ben Rogers—because naturally we’ve got to have a Gang, or there wouldn’t be any style to the thing. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—that sounds grand, don’t it, Huck?”

“Well, it certainly does, Tom. Who are we going to rob?”

“Oh, pretty much anybody. Lie in wait for people—that’s the usual way.”

“And murder them?”

“No, not every time. Shut them in the cave till they get a ransom together.”

“What’s a ransom mean?”

“Money. You make them get all they can out of their friends; and when you’ve kept them a year, if they haven’t raised it you kill them. That’s the ordinary rule. Except you never kill women. You keep the women locked up, but don’t kill them. They’re always rich and beautiful, and dreadful frightened. You take their watches and such things, but you always lift your hat and speak polite. Nobody’s as polite as robbers—you can find that in any book. Well, the women fall in love with you, and when they’ve spent a week or two in the cave they quit crying, and then you couldn’t make them go away. Drive them out and they’d come straight back again. That’s how all the books have it.”

“Why, that’s bully, Tom. I reckon it beats being a pirate.”

“Yes, some ways it’s better, because you’re near home and circuses and everything.”

Everything was ready by now, and the boys went into the hole, with Tom first. They worked their way to the tunnel’s farther end, secured their joined kite-strings, and went onward.

“I must leave without knowing my fate, but I will come back here, or follow your party, as soon as I can. A word or a look will tell me whether I am to enter your father’s house tonight or never again.”

She could not quickly recover from a letter like this. Half an hour alone to think might have calmed her, but she had only ten minutes before someone interrupted her. With all the demands of her situation, that was no time to find peace. Instead, every moment brought fresh excitement. Her happiness was overwhelming. Before the first rush of feeling had passed, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta all came in.

The need to seem her usual self immediately forced her to make an effort, but after a while she could not keep it up. She stopped understanding anything they said and had to explain that she felt unwell and ask to be excused. They now noticed how ill she looked, were alarmed and concerned, and would not dream of going anywhere without her. This was dreadful. If only they would leave her alone in that room, the quiet would cure her. Having them all stand or wait around her was unbearable, and in desperation she said she would go home.

“Certainly, my dear,” cried Mrs Musgrove. “Go home at once and look after yourself, so that you can be well for the evening. I wish Sarah were here to treat you, for I am no doctor myself. Charles, ring and ask them to order a carrying chair. She must not walk.”

But a chair was impossible. That would be worst of all! She could not bear to lose the chance of exchanging a few words with Captain Wentworth as she walked quietly up through the town alone. She felt almost certain she would meet him. She strongly opposed the chair. Mrs Musgrove, whose thoughts ran only to one kind of illness, anxiously made sure that Anne had not fallen: that she had not slipped recently and struck her head, and was quite certain no such fall had happened. Once satisfied, she could let Anne go cheerfully, confident of finding her better that evening.

Eager to leave nothing to chance, Anne made an effort and said—

“I am afraid, ma’am, that our invitation may not be entirely understood. Please tell the other gentlemen that we hope to see your whole party this evening. I fear there may have been a mistake, and I particularly wish you to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope they will both come.”

“Oh, my dear, everyone understands perfectly, I give you my word.
